Xerox Parc invented modern computing- mouse, icons, app windows, etc. That technology was suppressed by Xerox executives because it competed with Xerox's core business model of printing and intelligence services. Steve Jobs repurposed that tech and created new business model- mass consumer personal computing. It's that business model that changed the industry, not the tech.

Magnetic tape recording was invented in 1939 in Bell Laboratory. Again, the executives in charge suppressed the tech believing it would compete with their core business model of instant communication. In 1965, Philips repurposed the technology and invented the tape recorder and patented it, but their business model was narrow and non-transformative. In 1978 Sony repurposed the tape recorder business and released the Walkman. It became the transformative business model the tech needed to change the world. Sony maintained market dominance until Steve Jobs introduced the ipod at a fraction of the cost and an exponential growth rate in music storage and delivery capability over the magnetic tape.

This is the nature of all monopolies. Their business orthodoxies and corporate cultures make them slow to change and unadaptable to market forces- especially emergent market forces. If there is one law governing all market forces, including the Invisible Hand, it is that there will always be new emergent market forces. Emergent market forces are an inevitable consequence of universal entropy. Or in the words of Mao Zedong, "Capitalism contains the seeds of its own destruction, it is only a matter of time until the conditions will be right for the workers to rise in revolution and take over." The irony of his insight is that his Communist revolution would inevitably be taken over by capitalism itself. His insight wasn't right, but his vision and scope were wrong. He thought this principle only applied to capitalism, when it is really a universal systems principle. All systems contain within themselves the seeds of their own destruction.
